summary: Outlines issues and the nature of the problem of providing quality of service signaling across nested Virtual Private Networks, where the networks are sensitive about what information crosses boundaries while handling different precedence levels. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a private tunnel inside another private tunnel. Messages about priority need to cross between them without telling away secrets. This note describes the puzzle.

questions: how to signal qos in nested vpns
qos across nested virtual private networks
how does rsvp work across vpn boundaries
subtitle: Quality of service signals across encrypted nested tunnels

tldr.problem: Virtual Private Networks encrypt traffic so outsiders cannot see it, but sometimes one VPN is inside another, and both need to handle priority calls or critical traffic. The inner network wants to signal priority to its peers, but the outer network cannot see the encrypted traffic to make intelligent routing decisions.
tldr.mechanism: The memo uses RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol) and the Integrated Services model to describe how reservations for priority traffic can be made at boundaries between nested VPNs, with careful attention to what information crosses encryption boundaries and how preemption works when capacity runs out.
tldr.outcome: The framework allows networks to support quality of service for real-time applications like voice across nested encrypted tunnels without revealing the internal traffic or priorities to the outer network.

today: RFC 4923 is an informational memo describing frameworks for QoS in nested VPNs. While largely superseded by more modern approaches like Segment Routing and segment-based Traffic Engineering, the architectural principles—particularly separating policy from mechanism and handling precedence across trust boundaries—remain relevant to VPN design.

sections.title: The Problem of Quality of Service in Nested VPNs
sections.content:
Many organizations connect offices over the public internet by encrypting traffic—creating a VPN. Sometimes these networks are nested: an organization's internal encrypted network connects to a provider's encrypted network, which crosses the internet. The inner network knows which calls are urgent (voice, video conference) and which can tolerate delays (web browsing). But because the traffic is encrypted, the outer network cannot see which packets are important.

Real-time applications like voice and video cannot adapt to packet delays the way file transfers can. A call requires consistent, low-delay delivery; a file transfer will automatically slow down if capacity is tight and is happy to wait. Without quality of service, an urgent call may stall behind a bulk file transfer.

The challenge: the inner network needs to signal 'this traffic is important' to routers and VPN gateways at the boundary, without revealing what the traffic is or what it says.
sections.plainLanguage: You have two locked doors between you and the phone call. The first lock knows it's important to let the call through quickly. The second lock cannot read your message. So the first lock has to tell the second lock 'hurry up this one', without saying what it is.

sections.title: VPN Structure and QoS Technology
sections.content:
A nested VPN consists of two VPN routers on the encrypted network interface exchanging encrypted traffic. Inside the inner tunnel, hosts send normal IP traffic to a plaintext interface; the VPN router encrypts it and sends it across the outer network through a ciphertext interface.

Integrated Services (IntServ) divides applications into two types: real-time applications (voice, video) that need specific data rates and bounded delays, and elastic applications (file transfer, web) that adapt to available capacity. Real-time applications need guarantees; elastic applications just need bandwidth when available.

RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol) lets applications and the network negotiate about requirements. An application says 'I need 80 kilobits per second with low jitter for a voice call'; routers along the path agree or deny. RSVP supports both reservation (making space for the traffic) and preemption (removing lower-priority traffic if higher-priority traffic needs the space).
sections.plainLanguage: A VPN router takes your unencrypted traffic and locks it up before sending it. Real-time traffic (voice) says 'reserve me a lane'. Elastic traffic (downloads) takes whatever is left. The protocol RSVP lets the network say yes or no to reservations.

sections.title: Reservation and Preemption Across Boundaries
sections.content:
The memo describes in detail how RSVP reservations work in nested VPNs. When a voice call begins inside the inner network, the application (or a gateway) sends an RSVP request for capacity. The inner VPN router bundles this with other traffic and requests capacity across the outer VPN tunnel as an aggregate.

At the tunnel boundary, the VPN router acts as an aggregator: it combines individual reservations from many flows into one larger reservation for the tunnel. On the far side, the deaggregator splits the tunnel reservation back out.

If the outer network runs out of capacity, it can accept a higher-priority call by terminating a lower-priority one in a process called preemption. The key question the memo explores is: how does the router know which traffic to terminate? It cannot see inside the encrypted tunnel to know which flows are voice calls and which are file transfers. The answer involves using precedence levels (priority classes that can be embedded in headers at the tunnel boundary) and policy information (metadata about who is paying for priority service).
sections.plainLanguage: The router packages many calls together and says 'I need a big lane for this tunnel'. If it runs out of room, the outer network picks a lower-priority tunnel or flow to cancel to make space. The trick is doing this without decrypting the traffic.

sections.title: Data Flows and Implementation Approaches
sections.content:
The memo discusses two main ways VPN routers can handle data and signaling across the encryption boundary: directly, and using a Network Guard (a specialized device that enforces security policy).

In the direct approach, the router has both plaintext and ciphertext interfaces on the same device. It reads IP headers from the plaintext side to determine which flows need which priority, then encrypts them with appropriate QoS headers that the outer network can understand (while the data payload remains encrypted).

In the Network Guard approach, the plaintext router and the encryption device are separate. The plaintext router makes routing and QoS decisions based on unencrypted headers, then passes packets to the encryption unit, which adds security. This separation can improve security by keeping decryption keys away from the main routing logic.

Practical examples in the memo show how a routine voice call is reservedacross a nested VPN, step by step, from the application making the RSVP request through the routers making the reservations and finally being accepted by the outer network.
sections.plainLanguage: The router either reads the plaintext headers itself before encrypting, or hands them to a separate security device. Either way, it records 'this one is a voice call' before locking everything up, so the outer network can honor the priority.

sections.title: Security and Policy in Nested VPNs
sections.content:
The main security concerns are preventing spoofing (forgery of priority signals), ensuring only authorized users can request high-priority service, and validating that the information crossing the tunnel boundary is correct.

The memo emphasizes that QoS policy is separate from QoS mechanism. A router may use priority queuing as the mechanism (high-priority packets are sent first), but precedence levels determine which traffic actually gets priority. Precedence is a policy decision (which user or application deserves priority), while priority queuing is the technical implementation (which packets get sent first).

Protocols like RSVP with policy objects and integration with Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) help ensure that only authenticated users with appropriate policy can reserve capacity. RSVP preemption allows a network to selectively terminate service to enforce policies: a higher-precedence flash traffic call can preempt a routine call if needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the right people should be allowed to mark traffic as important. The routers use authentication and policy checking to verify 'yes, this user can request a priority lane' before honoring the reservation.
